sections.title: About
sections.line: I keep databases fast and make data searchable by meaning.
sections.body: Data has to be stored safely and come back out in milliseconds, ideally with the right answer. That’s my work, from database performance and vector search down to the systems underneath. And if there’s another layer under that, I’m going in.

sections.title: Learning
sections.line: What I’m reading and learning right now.

sections.title: Experience
sections.line: Where I’ve worked and what I did there.

sections.title: Vector search
sections.line: I build search that understands meaning, not just matching words.
sections.detail: Matryoshka embeddings pack most of their meaning into the first dimensions. An approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index built on only the first 128 or 64 dimensions finds 100 candidates, then the full 1024-dimension vectors rerank them to the top 5.

sections.title: Articles
sections.line: I write up what I test, so others can repeat it.
sections.closing: More write-ups exist but are internal to my employer.

sections.title: Database analysis
sections.line: I find out why a database is slow and fix it.
sections.detail: Most slow queries read far more data than they return. The query profile shows where the time goes; on a columnstore, a sort key that matches the filter lets the engine skip whole segments instead of scanning them.

sections.title: Open source
sections.line: When a tool breaks, I find out why and tell the people who can fix it.

sections.title: Agents
sections.line: I build AI assistants that can look things up and take actions.
sections.detail: An agent is an LLM in a loop: it plans, calls a tool (SQL, search, an API), reads the result, and decides what to do next until it can answer.

measured.caption: The database looked like it had memory to spare. Linux was quietly doing the caching.
measured.setup: On an on-premise SingleStore host with 7.5 GB RAM, I dropped the Linux page cache and ran two queries against a 33,554,432-row columnstore table.

runs.result: grew the page cache by only 9 MiB (answered from metadata).
took 4.20 s and grew the page cache by 66 MiB.

measured.conclusion: On-premise columnstore data is cached by the Linux page cache through buffered reads, so it never shows up in the database engine’s own memory metrics.
